textContent.text: Imagine traveling over three thousand miles of open ocean on a steamship no wider than an NBA basketball court. That was the incredible journey made by seventeen-year-old Annie Moore in late December of 1891. After twelve days at sea, the young immigrant from Ireland finally arrived on the shores of New York City, but her journey was not yet complete; before she could start her new life in America, Annie needed to visit a recently opened station for immigration inspection and processing. The station was known as Ellis Island, named after the small island on which it was located in New York Harbor. When Annie's name was marked in the registry book for new arrivals, she became the first of over twelve million immigrants to eventually pass through this historic point of entry.

Today, Ellis Island is no longer used for immigration purposes. Instead, it houses the Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration, which welcomes over three million visitors each year. Here, visitors can explore interactive exhibits, examine photographs and artifacts from the past, and conduct research on their own family's links to Ellis Island. In addition, the museum has been painstakingly restored to appear the way it did around 1918–1924. This helps visitors to vividly imagine the experience of immigrants who arrived during this time period.

pieces.text: The museum has three floors of exhibits on immigration at Ellis Island. When visitors enter the building, they step into a large, open vestibule known as the Baggage Room. In this room, antique suitcases line the walls and sit piled behind glass display cases. The suitcases, which are over a century old, encourage visitors to imagine a time when the room held the luggage of new immigrants. Next, on the second floor, is the Registry Room, a room with high, arched ceilings and long balconies on either side. On this floor, exhibits such as
describe in detail the steps new immigrants took to enter the United States through Ellis Island, such as medical screening and legal examination.
The third floor holds a visitor favorite: an exhibit called

. It features a variety of household objects like clothing and stuffed animals, as well as family documents that people carried with them as they traveled to the United States. These objects were donated to the museum by individuals who immigrated through Ellis Island or their families.
gives visitors today a more personal picture of how immigrants prepared for their new lives in an unfamiliar land.
The museum also offers visitors a chance to learn about immigration to the United States more broadly. Exhibits such as
provide a window into the history of American immigration going back as far as 1550. Meanwhile,
tells the story of immigration to the U.S. from 1945 on. This exhibit includes many videos and interactive displays. For example, in
, visitors can try to answer some of the questions asked on the naturalization test taken by residents applying for American citizenship.

textContent.text: The exhibits at the Ellis Island Museum have been designed to accommodate visitors with different needs. Ramps and elevators allow wheelchair users to access all parts of the museum. Tours are conducted in both English and American Sign Language, and self-guided audio tours are also available in over ten different languages. Visually impaired visitors can access informational booklets printed in braille, and there is even a small metal model of Ellis Island that visitors are encouraged to physically interact with. These features help to ensure that everyone who visits Ellis Island can enjoy the rich and detailed exhibits and learn about the fascinating history of immigration to the United States.

textContent.text: In southeastern Russia, just north of the Mongolian border, sits one of the world's most impressive bodies of water. Known as Lake Baikal, this banana-shaped lake is almost four hundred miles long and fifty miles wide. It is the sixth-largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area and the largest by volume. It is also the deepest freshwater lake in the world. This massive lake contains an astonishing one-fifth of all unfrozen fresh water found on the Earth's surface. In fact, if the lake were emptied out, the water from all five of the Great Lakes of North America would be able to fit inside it, with room left over!

Lake Baikal is located in Siberia, a sparsely populated region of Russia known for its long, harsh winters. For almost half the year, the lake is covered in ice that can reach over four feet thick, and even in the summertime, the average temperature is only around 52°F. Despite the chilly climate, however, Lake Baikal is incredibly biodiverse. It contains many endemic species—plants and animals that are found nowhere else on Earth. In fact, the lake is home to over 2,500 different plants and animals, and two-thirds of them are unique to Lake Baikal.

pieces.text: Although many plants and animals live in Lake Baikal, its waters are home to only one mammal: the Baikal seal. Also called the

by locals, the Baikal seal is the only seal in the world that lives exclusively in fresh water. Baikal seals have large close-set eyes, and strong claws they use to make breathing holes in the ice during the winter.
Another notable resident of the lake is the

. Copepods are minute crustaceans that survive by scavenging decaying bits of animal and vegetable matter. Thanks to the hard work of these tiny creatures, Lake Baikal is known for having some of the clearest water on Earth.

textContent.text: Despite this reputation for clear water, scientists and environmentalists have been raising concerns about pollution in the lake since at least 1966, when a pulp and paper mill was built on the shore of Lake Baikal. In the years that followed, many more factories were built in the surrounding areas, which caused further concern. While the copepods still keep Lake Baikal's water clear, they can't completely remove pollution from the water, and scientific studies have been documenting evidence of pollutants in the lake since at least the 1970s.

Fortunately, concerned citizens and environmental groups are working hard to protect Lake Baikal. They have lobbied for tighter regulation of nearby factories and protested against potentially harmful forms of development. They have also encouraged the growth of sustainable tourism in the area, promoting activities such as homestays, kayaking, and leave-no-trace hiking. These environmentalists hope that by teaching visitors to enjoy Lake Baikal responsibly, they can help preserve this unique and diverse natural resource for years to come.

pieces.text: When the Brazilian city of Rio de Janeiro was given its name, it was based on a misunderstanding. When Portuguese navigators had arrived on the southeastern coast of South America on January 1, 1502, they dropped anchor in what was actually the entrance to a large bay. At the time, though, they thought it was the mouth of a river. Therefore, they decided to name the area
, which is Portuguese for "January River."

textContent.text: Today, Rio de Janeiro is known worldwide for its rich culture and natural beauty. This alluring city is situated between lush, forested mountains and the shimmering expanse of the Atlantic Ocean; the busy and popular Guanabara Bay rests along the city's eastern edge. This location provides a striking backdrop for the many cultural events and activities for which Rio de Janeiro is famous.

Among the city's most well-known festivities is Carnival, an enormous annual celebration that starts in late February or early March. During Carnival, throngs of people flood the streets for almost an entire week of live music, dancing, and celebrations. For many people, the highlight of the festival is the Samba Parade, which takes place in a long, narrow building known as the Sambadrome. Tens of thousands of people pack into the Sambadrome to watch community groups called Samba Schools perform highly choreographed routines. These groups, dressed in elaborate, eye-catching costumes, sing, dance, and play the drums, hoping to be crowned the winners of the parade.

pieces.text: Some of the samba schools include capoeira performances in their routines.

is an Afro-Brazilian martial art with deep roots in Brazilian culture and history. It has at times also been described as a game or as a form of dance. A capoeira performance is characterized by fluid, acrobatic movements that include cartwheels, handstands, and rolls. Two
typically perform within a circle of spectators who clap, sing, and play rhythmic instruments. Everyone is expected to participate, which helps to foster a sense of community and respect.
Capoeira is not the only athletic pastime important to Brazilian culture.

, known in other parts of the world as soccer, is Brazil's national sport. Maracaña Stadium, one of the largest soccer stadiums in the world, can be found in Rio de Janeiro and is home to Brazil's national soccer team. Nicknamed the "Canary Squad" for their bright yellow jerseys, the team has produced some of the most famous soccer players in history, including the beloved Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known around the world by the nickname "Pelé." He is considered by many to be one of the greatest players of all time.

textContent.text: While Rio de Janeiro is famous for its rich cultural scene, the natural landscape also draws many visitors to the city. Rio de Janeiro's beaches are especially popular tourist destinations. Two of its most famous beaches are Copacabana Beach and Ipanema Beach, which are located on the southern side of the city, right on the edge of the Atlantic Ocean. Just miles away, Tijuca National Park offers over fifty miles of hiking trails to explore. Observant hikers can spot many different species of plants and animals, including several that are not found in any other protected area in the world. With stunning natural landscapes and rich cultural traditions, it's no wonder Rio de Janeiro is known as "the Marvelous City"!

title.text: The Royal Opera House Floral Hall, London

pieces.text: In the early 1700s, life in London was markedly different than it is today. There was no electricity, central heating, or running water. Much has changed since that time, but there is one thing that is still the same: the presence of a large theater positioned right in the heart of the city. Known today as the Royal Opera House, the theater was originally called the Theatre Royal (
being the British spelling of
). However, it was renamed when it was destroyed by fire and had to be almost entirely rebuilt—on two separate occasions!

As the name suggests, opera has played a large part in the history of the Royal Opera House, and to this day, the theater is world-famous for its opera performances. However, some people might be surprised to learn that when the theater first opened, opera wasn't the focus at all. For the first hundred or so years of its existence, it mostly functioned as a playhouse. It was only later that it also began to feature opera, along with ballet and pantomime, a type of musical comedy act. While plays and pantomimes eventually disappeared from the theater's stage, ballet became a major attraction that has persisted to the present day. In fact, over its long history, the theater's ballet company has employed four
, a title bestowed on the most exceptional or noteworthy dancers of their generation.

Though it is now an important cultural landmark, the Royal Opera House has not had an easy history. Apart from the two times when the building burned down, it was also forced to close on several other occasions. During World War I, the theater was temporarily claimed by the British government as a storehouse. It reopened in 1919, but came close to being completely torn down in 1927 to expand a nearby market. The planned demolition of the theater never happened, though, and the building remained standing. But the opera house closed yet again during World War II, when it was used as a dance hall. Finally, the Royal Opera House reopened on February 20, 1946, with a ballet performance of
. Since that time, it has largely remained open to the public, though it has undergone several major renovations to improve and expand the building.

textContent.text: Along with the renovations, the Royal Opera House has continued to innovate and adapt in other ways. The theater now offers a streaming service that allows viewers to watch ballet and opera productions from their own homes anywhere in the world. Since 2008, the Royal Opera House has also shown some of its opera and ballet broadcasts in movie theaters in places like the United Kingdom and Australia. And for those who are able to visit the theater in person, the venue offers tours and events. For example, there are behind-the-scenes tours, architecture tours, and even outdoor walking tours that lead visitors around the area surrounding the theater. By blending tradition with modernity in this way, the Royal Opera House continues to capture the imagination of dance and music lovers of all ages.

Known today as the Royal Opera House, the theater was originally called the Theatre Royal (

). However, it was renamed when it was destroyed by fire and had to be almost entirely rebuilt—on two separate occasions!

As the name suggests, opera has played a large part in the history of the Royal Opera House, and to this day, the theater is world-famous for its opera performances. However, some people might be surprised to learn that when the theater first opened, opera wasn't the focus at all. For the first hundred or so years of its existence, it mostly functioned as a playhouse. It was only later that it also began to feature opera, along with ballet and pantomime, a type of musical comedy act. title.text: Inside view of mission control center at the JPL

textContent.text: In 1936, a group of young researchers and rocket enthusiasts gathered in a dry, empty canyon northeast of Los Angeles. They had come to stage some daring experiments in rocketry, a field that was largely considered unscientific and even laughable in America at the time. But their hard work paid off when, just a few years later, they received funding from the U.S. Army to continue their experiments. In 1943, the group named itself the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). Fifteen years later, the JPL teamed up with NASA to design and build spacecraft.

Today, the JPL is run through an official partnership between NASA and the California Institute of Technology. The organization occupies a cluster of buildings at a site not far from where its first rocket experiments took place. One of these buildings is home to the Space Flight Operations Facility, where computers constantly monitor many different spacecraft. The JPL is responsible for operating NASA's Deep Space Network, the communication lifeline that transmits messages to and from spacecraft. Some of these spacecraft are over fourteen billion miles away! Incredibly, the Deep Space Network has been in operation twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week since 1964. The scientists at the JPL continue to work tirelessly to monitor and control NASA's interplanetary and deep space missions.

Another fascinating location within the JPL is the Machine Shop, where many spacecraft parts are built. A quick glance into the shop reveals just how much precision is required to build robotic spacecraft. The team uses incredibly well-maintained and precise machine tools, such as a lathe that can cut material accurately to 1/10,000 of an inch. The temperature and humidity in this area are strictly controlled in order to ensure that the hardware maintains its accuracy as the engineers and machinists work.

pieces.text: In the building where spacecraft are actually assembled, conditions are even more strictly controlled. This facility consists of two

. Anyone who enters either room is required to wear special clothing like gloves, masks, and head and shoe coverings. These safety measures protect the spacecrafts' sensitive equipment and electronics. In fact, reducing the risk of contamination is so important that one of the rooms is capable of filtering the air to contain less than one thousand particles of dust per cubic foot. These meticulous standards help ensure the success of the JPL's missions. Many of these missions involve robotic spacecraft, such as the Mars rover
. This rover, which landed on Mars in 2021, is just one of many robotic spacecraft assembled by the JPL.

textContent.text: The JPL is perhaps best known for its deep space and interplanetary missions, but the organization's work extends to practical applications here on Earth. At its Earth Satellite Mission Control Center, scientists use data from satellites orbiting the planet to collect information on global ice, sea level changes, and the Earth's surface temperature. Collecting this information helps NASA scientists understand more about how the planet's climate has changed over time. Whether it is observing our own planet or exploring the far reaches of space, the JPL continues to push the boundaries of scientific discovery and technological advancement.

But their hard work paid off when, just a few years later, they received funding from the U.S. Army to continue their experiments. In 1943, the group named itself the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). Fifteen years later, the JPL teamed up with NASA to design and build spacecraft.

Today, the JPL is run through an official partnership between NASA and the California Institute of Technology. The organization occupies a cluster of buildings at a site not far from where its first rocket experiments took place. One of these buildings is home to the Space Flight Operations Facility, where computers constantly monitor many different spacecraft. The JPL is responsible for operating NASA's Deep Space Network, the communication lifeline that transmits messages to and from spacecraft. Some of these spacecraft are over fourteen billion miles away! Incredibly, the Deep Space Network has been in operation twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week since 1964. The scientists at the JPL continue to work tirelessly to monitor and control NASA's interplanetary and deep space missions.

Another fascinating location within the JPL is the Machine Shop, where many spacecraft parts are built. A quick glance into the shop reveals just how much precision is required to build robotic spacecraft. The team uses incredibly well-maintained and precise machine tools, such as a lathe that can cut material accurately to 1/10,000 of an inch. The temperature and humidity in this area are strictly controlled in order to ensure that the hardware maintains its accuracy as the engineers and machinists work.

pieces.text: In the building where spacecraft are actually assembled, conditions are even more strictly controlled. This facility consists of two

. Anyone who enters either room is required to wear special clothing like gloves, masks, and head and shoe coverings. These safety measures protect the spacecrafts' sensitive equipment and electronics. In fact, reducing the risk of contamination is so important that one of the rooms is capable of filtering the air to contain less than one thousand particles of dust per cubic foot. These meticulous standards help ensure the success of the JPL's missions. Many of these missions involve robotic spacecraft, such as the Mars rover
. This rover, which landed on Mars in 2021, is just one of many robotic spacecraft assembled by the JPL.

textContent.text: The JPL is perhaps best known for its deep space and interplanetary missions, but the organization's work extends to practical applications here on Earth. At its Earth Satellite Mission Control Center, scientists use data from satellites orbiting the planet to collect information on global ice, sea level changes, and the Earth's surface temperature. Collecting this information helps NASA scientists understand more about how the planet's climate has changed over time. Whether it is observing our own planet or exploring the far reaches of space, the JPL continues to push the boundaries of scientific discovery and technological advancement.

content.text: Read the paragraph about the Japanese art of ippitsuryu. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: In the ancient Japanese tradition of ippitsuryu, an artist creates a painting of a dragon using an ink wash and brushes.
First, a fine brush is used to form the head of the dragon.
<atomic>Next, the artist forms the dragon's body by twisting and turning a larger brush in one continuous stroke, without raising it from the surface of the page.</atomic>
The artist does not lift the brush from the paper while creating the beast's body.

<atomic>By applying different amounts of pressure and adjusting the position of the brush, the artist creates an impression of fluid motion, as well as a scale-like effect along the length of the creature's body.</atomic>
Afterwards, the artist often adds details like whiskers and claws to give the dragon a fierce or fantastical appearance.

content.text: Read the paragraph about polydactyl cats. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: Seven, Bigfoot, and Thumbelina are all good names for cats with extra toes, a phenomenon caused by a harmless genetic mutation known as polydactyly.
Other common genetic mutations in cats result in stubby tails and folded ears.
Polydactyl cats have as many as nine toes on each paw, compared to the usual four or five.
<atomic>In the 1800s, these cats were popular with sailors, who believed the cats' extra toes made them better at catching mice and climbing.</atomic>
The sailors often brought the felines along with them on their journeys, causing the polydactyl mutation to spread.

<atomic>Today, polydactyl cats are especially common along the eastern coast of the United States and Canada, as well as in Wales and parts of England, the same regions frequented by their seafaring ancestors.</atomic>

content.text: Read the paragraph about an ancient Mesoamerican chocolate drink. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: <atomic>The sweet hot cocoa that we enjoy today is far removed from its origins in ancient Mesoamerica.</atomic>
Early versions of the drink were created by roasting and crushing beans from the cacao tree, then mixing them with water, chili peppers, vanilla, and other spices.
<atomic>Froth was then added to the beverage by pouring it back and forth between clay cups.</atomic>
The Mayans called the resulting drink xocolatl (pronounced show-koh-LATL), which translates to "bitter water."
This deep brown liquid played a central role in the cultures of the Mayans and the Aztecs, who incorporated it into funerals, marriages, and initiation rituals.
Many centuries later, the chocolate bar was invented in Europe.
<atomic>The Mayans believed that xocolatl held healing powers and could even provide warriors with strength and bravery in battle.</atomic>

At its peak, an estimated twenty thousand residents took shelter in Derinkuyu.
<atomic>The space included many of the same amenities as an above-ground city, including schools, living quarters, areas for cattle, and an extensive water storage system.</atomic>
While visiting Derinkuyu would be fascinating, I don't think I would enjoy living there.

text.text: <atomic>Aristarchus of Samos, a Greek astronomer and mathematician living in the third century BCE, developed several important theories about the universe.</atomic>
He is best known for promoting the idea that the Earth revolves around the sun.
This hypothesis, which is known as the heliocentric theory, accurately describes our solar system as it is understood today.
<atomic>In Aristarchus's time, however, the heliocentric theory was rejected by most other astronomers.</atomic>
At the time, most astronomers did not believe that the Earth revolved around the sun.
<atomic>They supported the more familiar geocentric theory, which asserts that the sun revolves around the Earth.</atomic>
Aristarchus's heliocentric model would not gain popularity for another seventeen hundred years, when it was revived by famed Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.

text.text: <atomic>Aristarchus of Samos, a Greek astronomer and mathematician living in the third century BCE, developed several important theories about the universe.</atomic>
He is best known for promoting the idea that the Earth revolves around the sun.
This hypothesis, which is known as the heliocentric theory, accurately describes our solar system as it is understood today.
<atomic>In Aristarchus's time, however, the heliocentric theory was rejected by most other astronomers.</atomic>
At the time, most astronomers did not believe that the Earth revolved around the sun.
<atomic>They supported the more familiar geocentric theory, which asserts that the sun revolves around the Earth.</atomic>
Aristarchus's heliocentric model would not gain popularity for another seventeen hundred years, when it was revived by famed Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.

content.text: Read the paragraph about the Native American snow snake competition. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: <atomic>In the traditional Native American game known as snow snake, players compete by throwing carved pieces of wood down a narrow track of snow.</atomic>
The wooden "snow snakes" are typically less than one inch thick and anywhere from four to ten feet long.
<atomic>The track needs to be smooth and slippery, and it is sometimes made by dragging a log through the snow.</atomic>
Players take turns tossing their snow snakes underhand so they glide smoothly down the track.
<atomic>Serious competitors often grease their snow snakes prior to throwing them, sometimes relying on secret family recipes passed down from one generation to the next.</atomic>
The one time I played, my snow snake did not make it very far down the track.
<atomic>With lots of practice and a little good luck, there's no telling how far your snow snake might travel.</atomic>

content.text: Read the paragraph about why raccoons wet their paws before eating. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: <atomic>When raccoons are getting ready to eat, they often dip their paws in water.</atomic>
<atomic>This behavior makes it appear as though the creatures have excellent hygiene.</atomic>
In reality, however, raccoons care less about cleanliness than they do about the way their meal feels.
<atomic>Raccoons rely heavily on their sense of touch, and they have significantly more nerve endings in their paws than most other mammals.</atomic>
<atomic>When raccoons wet their paws, these nerve endings become more sensitive.</atomic>
Their paws are most receptive to feelings and sensations when they are wet.
By "washing up" before they eat, raccoons can more easily identify whether they are holding something dangerous or delicious.

content.text: Read the paragraph about Poseidon's ribbon weed. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: <atomic>In 2022, scientists collected genetic samples from ten separate seagrass meadows in Australia's Shark Bay, hoping to discover how many different seagrass species lived in the area and how genetically similar they were.</atomic>
These researchers were shocked to learn that the samples were not only all members of the same species, they were all part of the same plant!
<atomic>Stretching across 112 miles, this patch of Poseidon's ribbon weed is the largest known plant in the world.</atomic>
Another example of an enormous plant is a group of interconnected quaking aspens found in Utah.
<atomic>Due to its genetic makeup, the ribbon weed is especially hardy, capable of surviving in an area with intense sunlight and dramatic temperature fluctuations.</atomic>
<atomic>In addition to being large and resilient, this plant is also quite old.</atomic>
Scientists estimate that it has been cloning itself and growing steadily larger for more than four thousand years.

text.text: In the ancient Japanese tradition of ippitsuryu, an artist creates a painting of a dragon using an ink wash and brushes.
First, a fine brush is used to form the head of the dragon.
<atomic>Next, the artist forms the dragon's body by twisting and turning a larger brush in one continuous stroke, without raising it from the surface of the page.</atomic>
The artist does not lift the brush from the paper while creating the beast's body.

<atomic>By applying different amounts of pressure and adjusting the position of the brush, the artist creates an impression of fluid motion, as well as a scale-like effect along the length of the creature's body.</atomic>
Afterwards, the artist often adds details like whiskers and claws to give the dragon a fierce or fantastical appearance.

text.text: <atomic>The sweet hot cocoa that we enjoy today is far removed from its origins in ancient Mesoamerica.</atomic>

The Mayans called the resulting drink xocolatl (pronounced show-koh-LATL), which translates to "bitter water."
This deep brown liquid played a central role in the cultures of the Mayans and the Aztecs, who incorporated it into funerals, marriages, and initiation rituals.
Many centuries later, the chocolate bar was invented in Europe.
<atomic>The Mayans believed that xocolatl held healing powers and could even provide warriors with strength and bravery in battle.</atomic>

content.text: Read the paragraph about polydactyl cats. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: Seven, Bigfoot, and Thumbelina are all good names for cats with extra toes, a phenomenon caused by a harmless genetic mutation known as polydactyly.
Other common genetic mutations in cats result in stubby tails and folded ears.
Polydactyl cats have as many as nine toes on each paw, compared to the usual four or five.
<atomic>In the 1800s, these cats were popular with sailors, who believed the cats' extra toes made them better at catching mice and climbing.</atomic>
The sailors often brought the felines along with them on their journeys, causing the polydactyl mutation to spread.

<atomic>Today, polydactyl cats are especially common along the eastern coast of the United States and Canada, as well as in Wales and parts of England, the same regions frequented by their seafaring ancestors.</atomic>

content.text: Read the paragraph about the Native American snow snake competition. Select the sentence that should be removed to improve the focus of the paragraph.

text.text: <atomic>In the traditional Native American game known as snow snake, players compete by throwing carved pieces of wood down a narrow track of snow.</atomic>
The wooden "snow snakes" are typically less than one inch thick and anywhere from four to ten feet long.
<atomic>The track needs to be smooth and slippery, and it is sometimes made by dragging a log through the snow.</atomic>
Players take turns tossing their snow snakes underhand so they glide smoothly down the track.
<atomic>Serious competitors often grease their snow snakes prior to throwing them, sometimes relying on secret family recipes passed down from one generation to the next.</atomic>
The one time I played, my snow snake did not make it very far down the track.
<atomic>With lots of practice and a little good luck, there's no telling how far your snow snake might travel.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Aristarchus of Samos, a Greek astronomer and mathematician living in the third century BCE, developed several important theories about the universe.</atomic>
He is best known for promoting the idea that the Earth revolves around the sun.
This hypothesis, which is known as the heliocentric theory, accurately describes our solar system as it is understood today.
<atomic>In Aristarchus's time, however, the heliocentric theory was rejected by most other astronomers.</atomic>

Colorado is home to fifty-eight mountains that rise fourteen thousand feet or higher above sea level. These majestic peaks, proudly known as the 14ers, offer many opportunities for outdoor exploration. They are popular destinations for hikers, rock climbers, and skiers. Stargazers also seek out these isolated mountaintops as places to search the sky. Likewise, many adventurers flock to the 14ers to watch the uniquely adapted wildlife that thrives at these extreme elevations.
